frameworks.name: Process-Goal Reframe
frameworks.definition: Replace outcome goals (sell X copies) with process goals (four hours of promotion per day); judge success by adherence to committed actions, not external results.

frameworks.name: Give in Public, Sell in Private
frameworks.definition: Maintain high-value public content to build goodwill and audience growth; reserve direct commercial asks for private DM conversations when a prospect has already signaled interest.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that a person asking for a market guarantee before taking action is asking the universe for a response the universe will never give; the only party that always responds is the marketplace, which answers every knock on the door with either acceptance or rejection.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: The marketplace is the only entity whose response is guaranteed because it is driven by real demand, whereas internal deliberation and pre-launch analysis produce only silence.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that outcome-focused goal-setting for activities with uncertain results (such as book sales) creates unnecessary fear because the individual cannot control the outcome; shifting the commitment to controllable process actions (e.g., four hours of daily promotion) makes success measurable regardless of market result.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Goal outcome depends on market response (e.g., book sales, product launches)
Individual has full control over input actions
claims.mechanism: When the goal is framed as an outcome, failure is determined by market forces outside the individual's control, creating fear and paralysis; when the goal is framed as a daily process commitment, success is determined entirely by behavior, eliminating the fear driver.
bounded_by: Does not apply when the outcome is directly within the individual's control (e.g., internal operational tasks)

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that skills and marketing knowledge developed during an unsuccessful product launch are themselves the real output of the attempt; a creator who reaches 100 sales instead of 1,000 will identify the one or two channels that work and can then repeat or scale those on the next project.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: First or early-stage product launch
Creator has not previously mapped which promotion channels generate the most sales
claims.mechanism: Market feedback on a failed attempt reveals the winning channels by elimination, which compound on subsequent attempts; the attempt is therefore a learning investment with guaranteed informational return.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi states that continuing to live through personal hardship is self-proving: the fact that a person is still showing up and working is itself evidence that they are already succeeding at the thing they claim they do not know how to do (survive and keep going).
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Individual is experiencing acute personal losses (bereavement, relationship breakdown) while maintaining professional obligations

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that the length of time required to recover emotionally from a loss (including a breakup or bereavement) is exactly as long as the individual decides it takes; recovery timeline is a decision variable, not a fixed biological process.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that a person's difficult personal experiences become the stories they will eventually tell, and compelling personal narratives require real adversity; an entrepreneurial story without hardship is neither memorable nor relatable.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Audiences relate to struggle because it mirrors their own experience; a straight-line success story provides no emotional resonance or instructional value.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi recommends that content creators with an audience should give value publicly and convert commercially only in private conversations (DMs, reply to story interactions) rather than aggressive public calls-to-action; a light-touch CTA (story prompt or comment invite to book a call) preserves audience goodwill while still generating revenue.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.speaker_term: give in public sell in private
conditions: Creator has an existing audience with strong engagement (comments, DMs)
Creator runs a service-based business reliant on community goodwill
Creator does not want to damage audience trust with aggressive promotion
claims.mechanism: Public aggressive selling signals transaction intent and erodes the social contract that underlies audience loyalty; private outreach respects the audience member's agency and mirrors a natural conversation rather than a pitch.
bounded_by: Does not apply to pure direct-response advertisers who have no pre-existing community relationship

claims.text: Alex Hormozi states that pursuing multiple business paths simultaneously (brick-and-mortar, online, new digital product) virtually guarantees failure at all of them, because capital and attention are limited and each path demands full commitment to reach escape velocity.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Individual is at an early growth stage with limited capital and time
Business paths are operationally distinct (different skills, channels, customer bases)
claims.mechanism: When attention is divided, progress on each path is slower than competitors pursuing only that path, and cash flow disruptions in one path pull attention back from the others, creating a feedback loop of mediocrity across all.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that a fitness business owner whose in-person business is running well should scale to a second physical location before going online, because their existing two years of operating knowledge compounds as a durable advantage in the same vertical; going online restarts their learning curve from zero.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Brick-and-mortar business is already profitable and operationally stable
Owner has two or more years of domain experience in their current model
Owner has zero established track record or audience in the online channel
claims.mechanism: Knowledge within a vertical compounds non-linearly over time; switching to a new channel discards existing compounding and restarts a new, slower compounding curve. The wealthiest operators Hormozi knows have spent 40+ years in one space.
bounded_by: Does not apply if the current model is fundamentally unscalable (e.g., requires owner's physical presence at all times)

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that owning multiple brick-and-mortar locations without being physically present in any of them is achievable, and the belief that online-only is necessary to achieve location independence is a false assumption; he personally owns approximately 70 brick-and-mortar locations across different companies without being on-site in any of them.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Owner has built systems, hired management, and incentivized staff appropriately

numbers.axis: number of brick-and-mortar locations owned without owner on-site presence

anchors.region: owner who must be physically present

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that a solo entrepreneur in a commoditized professional service (bookkeeping, accounting) whose prior business stalled did not fail because of their skill or the demand for their service, but because they did not spend sufficient time on promotion; for solo service providers, 100% of revenue is profit and the binding constraint is letting enough people know about the service.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Solo service provider with no employees
Commoditized service with proven demand (bookkeeping, accounting, CFO services)
Prior business relied primarily on referrals
claims.mechanism: Solo professional service has near-100% gross margin because there are no employees; revenue is directly proportional to the number of people who know the service exists; low-velocity referral pipelines stall when one client churns before a new referral arrives.
bounded_by: Does not apply when the service itself is undifferentiated and commoditized to the point of pure price competition

claims.text: Alex Hormozi recommends that a solo accounting/bookkeeping entrepreneur target 10,000 direct outreach contacts to build a stable client base; contacting 10,000 business owners produces enough conversions to establish the volume of clients needed for full-time income.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Solo professional service provider (bookkeeping, accounting, CFO services)
No existing audience or established referral engine
Target clients are business owners who need financial services

numbers.axis: number of outreach contacts required to establish full-time client base for a solo accounting business

anchors.region: direct cold outreach to business owners
B2B partnership outreach (adjacent businesses referring clients)

claims.text: Alex Hormozi states that in the early stage of a content-based business, organic content functions as lead nurture rather than lead generation; most early clients will come from direct outreach, not content; content ROI as a lead source may take one to two years to materialize.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Creator is early-stage with a small or non-existent audience
Creator is relying on content as their primary lead source
claims.mechanism: Early-stage audiences are too small to generate sufficient inbound volume; content serves to validate credibility when outbound prospects check the creator's profile, which then improves the conversion rate of direct outreach.

numbers.axis: time to content-driven lead generation ROI for early-stage solo professional

anchors.region: content as lead nurture (supports outreach conversion)
content as primary lead generation source

bounded_by: Does not apply to creators who already have large audiences (100k+) where inbound volume is sufficient

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that a person who wants to build a world-changing technology company (comparable to Amazon, Facebook, or Microsoft) without existing capital or investor backing faces an improbably high barrier because every one of those reference companies was founded by already well-capitalized individuals (Bezos was a Wall Street banker; Gates came from a wealthy family; Zuckerberg attended Harvard); the advice to start small and build sustainable income first is not discouragement but a path to staying solvent long enough to attempt the larger vision.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Solo entrepreneur with no investors and limited personal capital
Targeting a highly competitive, capital-intensive market (social network, ecommerce platform, enterprise software)
claims.mechanism: World-changing companies require being able to sustain operations for 10-20+ years without revenue; without capital access, the entrepreneur cannot stay in the game long enough for the compounding to materialize.

numbers.axis: company age of major tech platforms at the time of reference

bounded_by: Does not apply to capital-light software businesses where the founder can reach revenue quickly

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that strategy is fundamentally the prioritization of limited resources against unlimited options; the primary failure mode of early-stage entrepreneurs is defining the problem too broadly, which spreads limited resources below the threshold required to solve any one problem completely.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Early-stage entrepreneur with limited capital and no team
claims.mechanism: Resources below a minimum threshold on any single problem produce zero useful output; concentrated resources on a narrow problem produce compounding returns as the problem gets solved and adjacent problems become accessible.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that the loneliness that growth-oriented entrepreneurs experience is a predictable, universal phase: they become too advanced for their existing social circle but have not yet proven themselves enough to enter the circle they aspire to, creating an in-between gap that every person who achieves anything material passes through.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Entrepreneur is actively growing and distancing from prior peer group
Entrepreneur has not yet established a new peer group at their next level

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that the quality filter for friends at high levels of achievement reduces to two criteria: do they make me better, and do they have my best interests at heart; these two criteria are independently difficult to satisfy and together constitute a very high bar.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

anchors.value: has my best interests at heart

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that high-achieving peers operate with zero social obligation around response time; within peer groups of similarly ambitious people, not responding to a text for three days generates no drama because everyone in the group understands that busy people are doing meaningful work.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Both parties are actively building demanding businesses or careers
The friendship is at a mature stage with established mutual understanding
bounded_by: Does not apply in early-stage friendships where trust has not yet been established
Does not apply to personal relationships where emotional support obligations exist

claims.text: Alex Hormozi states that comfort, while beneficial in creating a stable business community, is the enemy of achievement and growth; the fact that the comfortable path feels easy is a signal that it is producing insufficient challenge and therefore insufficient compounding.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.speaker_term: comfort is the enemy of achievement and growth
bounded_by: Does not imply that discomfort alone produces growth; the discomfort must be directed at productive challenges

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that for a solo entrepreneur who returned to a 9-to-5 after a failed business attempt, the primary fix is dedicating four hours of promotion per day during nights and weekends; a competent solo bookkeeper who does four hours of daily promotion (content creation and direct outreach) will have more business than they can handle within six months.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Solo professional service provider with a validated, in-demand skill (bookkeeping, CFO services)
Individual already holds a day job and is rebuilding business on the side
Promotion consists of content creation and direct outreach, not paid ads (due to financial constraints)
claims.mechanism: The solo service provider's prior failure was a promotion-volume problem, not a skill problem; increasing promotion volume to four hours per day creates enough pipeline that even a low conversion rate produces sufficient clients to reach full-time income.

numbers.axis: time to achieve stable solo bookkeeping client base given four hours of daily promotion

anchors.value: stalls at 1-3 clients, collapses when any client churns

anchors.region: promotion volume: four hours per day (content + outreach)

examples.text: A writer who ghostwrites for celebrities and CEOs (following Hormozi's prior advice to write for wealthy clients) wants to self-publish her next book with a goal of 1,000 ebook sales. She is paralyzed by having too many execution paths (Amazon, ClickFunnels, etc.) and fears repeating past self-publishing attempts that did not hit her target. Hormozi reframes her goal: instead of targeting 1,000 copies as the measure of success, she should commit to four hours of daily promotion and judge success by adherence to that commitment. He also suggests reaching out to 1,000 people with relevant audiences, noting that if even one person per contact sells 20 books, the volume makes 1,000 sales likely.

A business speaker traveled to London to keynote Europe's largest business event. On his first day of arrival, his grandfather passed away. He maintained his composure, delivered the speech with a smile in front of thousands, then flew back and buried his grandfather. He also had his grandmother battling cancer and had recently ended a serious relationship. He asks Hormozi how to maintain composure. Hormozi responds: you have already answered your own question by doing the thing you claim not to know how to do. The fact that you are here asking the question is evidence you have already succeeded at surviving.

Phil Knight's Shoe Dog documents 30 years of Phil Knight being repeatedly knocked down — supplier failures, financing crises, legal disputes — before Nike became a global brand. Hormozi cites this as the template for compelling entrepreneurial stories: the entire narrative is adversity, with success appearing only at the very end. If Knight's story were a straight line to scale, no one would care about it.

A fitness business owner in a small beach town has been running a popular in-person gym for two years. He wants to achieve location independence so he can live elsewhere for part of the year. He assumes this requires going online. Hormozi corrects the assumption: he personally owns approximately 70 brick-and-mortar locations across different companies and is not physically present in any of them. The path to location independence is to delegate and systematize the first gym, not to abandon the model.

Facebook did not start as a platform to connect the entire world. Mark Zuckerberg started by mapping colleges. Amazon started by selling only books. Both eventually expanded outward to adjacent problems once they had solved the initial narrow problem completely. Hormozi uses these examples to argue that a solo entrepreneur with no capital who wants to build the next Amazon should instead pick one narrow problem, solve it completely, then expand.

A former full-time entrepreneur with four children under five and significant business debt returned to a 9-to-5 after his bookkeeping and CFO services business stalled. His prior business grew primarily via referrals, giving him one to three clients at most; whenever one churned, the business collapsed before the next referral arrived. Hormozi diagnoses the failure as a promotion-velocity problem, not a skill or market problem, and prescribes 10,000 direct outreach contacts (or 1,000 B2B partnership pitches) plus one post per day of content, dedicating four hours nightly to promotion.

An entrepreneur growing revenue from $25K per month to higher levels describes feeling increasingly lonely as he became more successful; old friends could not relate to his journey and new peers at the level he aspired to had not yet accepted him. Hormozi validates this as a universal experience: every person who achieves anything material passes through this exact gap between social circles. He recommends physically relocating to a fitness-centric city (the individual was moving to Kelowna, BC) and joining online communities of people in the same space, starting by giving value to those communities before asking for anything.

practices.text: When analyzing whether to scale a brick-and-mortar business or pivot online, test your systems first by stepping away from your existing location for a year; if the business runs without you, you have proven scalability and can choose either path. If it does not run without you, fix that before any expansion.

For a solo professional service provider with limited capital, spend nights and weekends (four hours per night) on promotion: one post per day plus direct outreach. Do not spend on paid ads until the free channels (content and cold outreach) are saturated.

When building a new peer group as a growth-oriented entrepreneur, identify givers in communities by watching who contributes without asking for anything first; givers recognize givers. Start by providing value to the community before requesting introductions or help.

Judge yourself on what you do, not on how you feel; you can feel terrible and still show up with a smile in front of a thousand people. Separate behavioral output from emotional state as the primary measure of performance.

For a content creator with an existing engaged audience, use story CTAs and comment invitations to book a call as the sales mechanism; do not broadcast aggressive public pitches that damage the goodwill already established.
